results.correct_value: Descent reverses the Sherman summit snow / West Ridge to the crater rim, then the Easton Glacier; the Roman Wall is not on this route
results.evidence: Easton route descriptions place the Roman Wall above Sherman Crater, between the crater and Baker's summit plateau. The Sherman Peak route goes right at the crater rim, around a jagged high point and up the West Ridge to Sherman's summit, never touching the Roman Wall. The row's descent, beta and approach_variants agree; descent_text was written for Baker's summit.

patches.find: downclimb the steep snow of the upper Easton Glacier past the Roman Wall section first — most parties find this the psychologically hardest part of the day simply because of sustained steepness (roughly 30 degrees) right off the summit plateau;

results.fact: Sherman Peak bearing from Grant Peak
results.correct_value: Sherman Peak is about two-thirds of a mile (1 km) due south of Grant Peak
results.evidence: A topo peak database places Sherman Peak at 48.7672 N, 121.8139 W, 1.0 km from its parent Mount Baker; Mount Baker's summit is at 48.7766 N, 121.8145 W, which puts Sherman ~1.05 km almost due south (about 40 m east). An encyclopedia photo caption describes looking south into Sherman Crater from Grant Peak. Both 'southeast' and 'southwest' are off; 'half a mile' understates ~0.65 mi.

results.fact: Line to the summit (Roman Wall saddle vs south ridge)
results.evidence: A club route page says to make a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge and climb steep snow on the ridge (matching the camp card); a club trip report noted that south-ridge line was snow-free and not feasible in August. Other Squak descriptions lead toward the Roman Wall / Easton line under Sherman Crater, which is Baker's summit route; the row's beta (saddle below the Roman Wall, rime-knob ridge) likely comes from one party's variant. Only one source states the Sherman line explicitly, and the bivy card is out of scope for patches.

results.correct_value: The Squak is chiefly an early-season climb; a bergschrund develops across the route as the season goes on
results.evidence: The Forest Service Squak route page says the Squak is limited to early-season climbing because a bergschrund develops along the route as the season progresses. A guide service calls it the best route for early season because a hard-to-navigate bergschrund can develop later. The season chip Jun-Sep is left as the outer window; the prose that calls June-September the most stable period is corrected.

patches.find: June-September is the primary climbing season with the most stable glacier-travel conditions.
